situation the courts faced during the “War on Terror.” In response to the 
terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, Congress enacted an Authorization for 
Use of Military Force (AUMF) that the Supreme Court interpreted to authorize 
the military to detain “enemy combatants.” See Hamdi v. Rumsfeld, 542 U.S. 
507, 516-24 (2004). The statute neither defined “enemy combatant” nor 
required any procedure for the government to use to classify individuals as 
“enemy combatants” or for those individuals to challenge their enemy-
combatant status. The Supreme Court held that Article III courts had 
jurisdiction to consider habeas petitions filed by persons detained as enemy 
combatants. See id.; Rasul v. Bush, 542 U.S. 466 (2004) (decided on the same 
day as Hamdi). But what process was due? On one side, the government 
resisted full tri al-h Fa procedures based on its interest “in detaining those who 
Actually pose an immediate threat to the national security of the United States 
during ongoing international conflict.” Hamdi, 542 U.S. at 530. On the other 
side, Yaser Hamdi (and other detainees) demanded greater procedural 
formality to protect “the most elemental of fiberty interests—the interest in 
being free from physical detention” by the government. Id. at 529. Although 
these extraordinary interests would seem to brook no compromise, a divided 
Supreme Court apphed Mathews and forged a middle procedural course for 
federal courts to follow when a person classified as an enemy combatant 
challenged his detention.
The political branches’ response to Hamdi and Rasul suggested 
dissatisfaction with the Supreme Court’s balancing of interests and resulting 
procedural specifications. Seven days after the Supreme Court’s decisions. 
Deputy Secretary of Defense Paul Wolfowitz issued an order establishing 
combatant status review tribunals (CSRTs) at Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, 
where the detainees were being held. Presumably, the goal was to provide an 
administrative alternative to satisfy due process. And yet the order avowedly 
was “intended solely to improve management” of Guantanamo and not to 
“create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law, in 
equity, or otherwise by any party against the United States, its departments, 
agencies, instrumentahties or entities, its officers, employees or agents, or any 
other person.” When it enacted the Defense Appropriation Act for fiscal year 
2006, Congress modestly reformed the CSRT process, including by providing 
for review of CSRT findings by a civilian officer of the Department of Defense 
who was appointed as a principal officer. Congress also stripped the federal 
courts of jurisdiction to review combatant status by habeas corpus or 
otherwise, while providing for an extremely limited form of review in the Court 
of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.
The resulting regime came under the Supreme Court’s scrutiny in 
Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 (2008). The Court held that the hmited scope 
of judicial review might have been adequate if the underlying CSRT procedures 
satisfied due process. But, again applying the Mathews formula, the Court 
concluded that the CSRT procedures were constitutionally inadequate. This 
did not end the matter. The dispute has continued—^through executive orders.
